title: Finding a Protein's Shape in Spots

scenes.tts: Where does each atom sit? Chemistry gives a protein's composition and sequence, not its fold. By nineteen ninety-one, nobody had seen the shape of the P K A catalytic subunit. Shape tells you function. In the early nineteen forties, biochemists had no method for molecules of thousands of atoms. Kendrew judged X-ray crystallography the only one with any chance.
scenes.visual: A protein outline under a question mark with the question where does each atom sit; composition and sequence shown as text chips that cannot show the fold; a thousands-of-atoms note; X-ray crystallography chip arrives.

scenes.tts: Grow the pure protein into a crystal. Kendrew chose myoglobin because it was small, easy to prepare in quantity, and readily crystallized. Good conditions are hard to predict, so you screen many solutions. Inside the crystal, the molecules sit in a regular lattice.
scenes.visual: One protein outline becomes a grid of drops, one drop grows a crystal, and the crystal is zoomed into a lattice of many identical outlines.
scenes.narration: Grow the pure protein into a crystal. Kendrew chose myoglobin because it was small, easy to prepare in quantity, and readily crystallized. Good conditions are hard to predict, so you screen many solutions. Inside the crystal, the molecules sit in a regular lattice.

scenes.tts: Keep the crystal wet and mounted, and shine a narrow beam of X-rays through it, rotating the crystal. X-rays scatter from the electrons around each atom. In some directions the scattering adds up. In others it cancels. The crystal sends the beam into a regular pattern of spots. Their positions reflect how the molecules are arranged. Their intensities depend on the atoms inside each molecule.
scenes.visual: Mounted crystal, beam in from the left, rotation arrow; waves add in some directions and cancel in others; a detector grid of spots, bright and dim.
scenes.narration: Keep the crystal wet and mounted, and shine a narrow beam of X-rays through it, rotating the crystal. X-rays scatter from the electrons around each atom. In some directions the scattering adds up. In others it cancels. The crystal sends the beam into a regular pattern of spots. Their positions reflect how the molecules are arranged. Their intensities depend on the atoms inside each molecule.

scenes.tts: The detector records only each spot's intensity. The phase of each wave is lost. That is the phase problem: half the information needed to make the image is missing. Perutz and Kendrew solved it with heavy atoms, for example mercury, attached at a few sites. Two or more such crystals fix the phases. Add up all the spots as waves, and you get an electron-density map.
scenes.visual: Each spot gets an intensity bar and a phase dial that is wiped out to a question mark; heavy-atom tags at a few sites shift the bars; the spots sum into a contour map.
scenes.narration: The detector records only each spot's intensity. The phase of each wave is lost. That is the phase problem: half the information needed to make the image is missing. Perutz and Kendrew solved it with heavy atoms, for example mercury, attached at a few sites. Two or more such crystals fix the phases. scenes.tts: Read the map as contours of density. Build a model into it, and refine it. Wide-angle spots carry the fine detail, so resolution depends on how far out the pattern is recorded. In Kendrew's myoglobin, at six angstroms you see rods of chain and one flat disc, the haem. At two angstroms, helices appear as hollow cylinders and the iron sits out of the haem plane. At one point four angstroms, bonded neighbours are only just resolved: the limit for these crystals.
scenes.visual: A contour map with a labelled model outline fitted in; a radius circle on the spot pattern; the map redrawn at 6, 2 and 1.4 angstroms with labels; schematic tag.
scenes.caption: Read the map as contours of density. Build a model into it, and refine it. Wide-angle spots carry the fine detail, so resolution depends on how far out the pattern is recorded. At 1.4 Å, bonded neighbours are only just resolved: the limit for these crystals.

scenes.tts: No crystal, no structure: a crystal that diffracts is often the chief barrier. Screen many conditions, or add a binding partner. A map made with model phases tends to show density where the model has it, and an incorrect model can still refine to a fairly good R value. Leave about ten percent of the spots out. Their R free value guards against over-fitting.
scenes.visual: Left: no-crystal drops with two workarounds. Right: model bias loop (model gives phases, map shows the model), then the reflection set split with R-free on the held-out tenth.

scenes.tts: In the late nineteen fifties, Kendrew's team built the first protein structure, myoglobin. A two angstrom map was published in nineteen sixty. Perutz compared oxygen-carrying horse haemoglobin with oxygen-free human haemoglobin at five point five angstroms. Two beta subunits rearranged, their separation changing by over seven angstroms. The two forms differ in quaternary structure.
scenes.visual: Two panels with source tags: myoglobin outline with first protein structure and a 2 angstrom tag; deoxy and oxy subunit-pair outlines side by side with a displacement arrow.
scenes.caption: In the late 1950s, Kendrew's team built the first protein structure, myoglobin. A 2 Å map was published in 1960. Perutz compared oxygen-carrying horse haemoglobin with oxygen-free human haemoglobin at 5.5 Å. Two beta subunits rearranged, their separation changing by over 7 Å. The two forms differ in quaternary structure.

scenes.tts: In nineteen ninety-one, Knighton, Taylor, Sowadski and colleagues solved the first protein kinase structure, of P K A, at two point seven angstroms: two lobes with a cleft. In nineteen ninety-eight, MacKinnon's lab solved the potassium channel KcsA at three point two angstroms, with a selectivity filter twelve angstroms long. Keep this rule. A shape in a crystal is a clue, so test it in cells.
scenes.visual: Two panels with source tags: two-lobed kinase outline with a cleft; channel filter outline with 12 angstrom span; then the rule appears in a box.
scenes.caption: In 1991, Knighton, Taylor, Sowadski and colleagues solved the first protein kinase structure, of PKA, at 2.7 Å: two lobes with a cleft. In 1998, MacKinnon's lab solved the potassium channel KcsA at 3.2 Å, with a selectivity filter 12 Å long. Keep this rule. A shape in a crystal is a clue, so test it in cells.
